title: Democrats Unite on Costs but Split Over Trump and the Path Forward After Midterm Sweep
dek: At a two-day conference in Denver, Democrats agreed on lowering costs but disagreed on how far to push the agenda and whether to work with President Trump.
author: Meridian Newsroom

image.alt: The Colorado State Capitol building in Denver

keyPoints: Democrats met in Denver for the What's Next conference, their first major gathering since the November 3 midterm wins, Reuters reported.
Speakers agreed on relieving voters of high costs but disagreed on the method, from a bolder progressive agenda to a move toward the center.
Ro Khanna urged a bolder agenda; Josh Shapiro argued for moving beyond ideological litmus tests, according to Reuters.
Asked whether delivering for voters includes working with Trump, Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand said, "Yes, because he's there," Colorado Politics reported.
Reuters noted that Trump retains veto power for two more years.
body:
Democrats gathered in Denver this week for their first major conference since the November 3 midterm elections, and came away united on one goal and divided on nearly everything else. Reuters reported that the party wants to give voters relief from high costs, but disagrees about how to get there, what lessons to take from its victory and how hard to push back against President Donald Trump.

## Shared goal, competing prescriptions

The two-day What’s Next conference was hosted by Majority Democrats, a group that advocates for younger party leaders. [Reuters reported](https://www.streetinsider.com/Reuters/After+midterm+sweep%2C+Democrats+split+over+Trump%2C+cost-cutting+agenda/27346166.html) that speakers disagreed over whether to embrace a bolder progressive agenda or tack toward the center. California Rep. Ro Khanna urged Democrats to stop chasing the political center and to back universal health care, a wealth tax, a $25 federal minimum wage, deep Pentagon cuts and the abolition of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a moderate and another potential 2028 contender, argued that the party should move beyond ideological litmus tests, saying voters “don’t give a damn” about such debates, according to Reuters. Strategist Elaine Kamarck told Reuters that the debate is likely to be large because the victory “was so broad it swept in centrists, southern Democrats and more progressive and left-wing Democrats.”

## Working with a president who still has power

The harder question was whether to cooperate with Trump. [Colorado Politics reported](https://coloradopolitics.com/2026/11/13/working-with-trump-democrats-dare-each-other-to-try-at-denver-event/) that strategists and lawmakers at the conference argued the party should work on areas of common ground, saying the risk of not doing so is too high. Iowa Democratic Gov.-elect Rob Sand, asked on the sidelines whether delivering for voters included working with Trump, said, “Yes, because he’s there.”

Reuters noted that Trump retains veto power for two more years, which keeps the question of cooperation or confrontation at the center of the debate. Colorado Politics reported that House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, speaking at a welcome event on Thursday night, said Democrats must make the country affordable for every American and hold officials accountable for what he called corruption.

## A warning about the mandate

Stephanie Valencia, co-founder of Equis Research, told attendees, according to Colorado Politics: “Our party is on probation with voters, who might not like us very much or know exactly what we stand for, but who have given us a chance anyway.” She added, “We maybe have the next year to 18 months to show voters who we are, or the pendulum might swing right back.”

## What remains open

Reuters described the conference as the opening of a contest over the party’s direction and its 2028 presidential standard-bearer, with prospective candidates and senior leaders debating how to turn the election into a governing agenda. The reporting reviewed for this story does not describe a consensus agenda, and Meridian has not confirmed any specific policy commitments made at the conference beyond those quoted above.
